new_topics.label: Expedited partner therapy: prescription validity and dispensing
HIPAA individual access: formats, fees and response requirements

questions.topic: Expired pharmacist registration: reactivation versus automatic renewal
questions.stem: A pharmacist allowed a Massachusetts registration to expire on December 31, 2022, but has continuously practiced under an unrestricted New Hampshire license. In November 2026, the pharmacist wants to resume work in a Massachusetts community pharmacy. Neither license has been suspended or revoked, and no military-service extension or waiver applies. The pharmacist can document the required continuing education and pay the outstanding fees. Which statement BEST describes the Massachusetts reactivation requirements?

choices.text: The pharmacist must complete the reactivation process, pass the MPJE, and satisfy the Board's other conditions before resuming Massachusetts practice.
choices.why: Under 247 CMR 4.02(5), an otherwise nondisciplinary registration that has expired for more than two years requires passing the MPJE and meeting Board conditions before renewal. The current Massachusetts Pharmacist Licensing page describes reactivation application approval followed by MPJE eligibility. Active practice in another state does not itself reactivate the Massachusetts registration.

choices.text: Payment of the overdue fees and proof of current CE restore authority to practice as soon as a complete application is submitted.
choices.why: Submitting the application and paying fees do not establish an active Massachusetts registration. The greater-than-two-year lapse invokes the additional requirements of 247 CMR 4.02(5). Practicing while the registration remains expired is unlicensed practice under 4.02(3).

choices.text: Continuous practice under the New Hampshire license eliminates the MPJE requirement, although the pharmacist must still submit CE and fees.
choices.why: The greater-than-two-year expiration rule does not contain an automatic MPJE exemption for a pharmacist who has practiced in another jurisdiction. Other-state license verification is part of the reactivation process, not a substitute for the required examination.

choices.text: Every pharmacist whose registration has expired for more than two years must automatically retake both the NAPLEX and the MPJE.
choices.why: Section 4.02(5) expressly requires the MPJE and other Board-determined conditions; it does not automatically mandate the NAPLEX for every nondisciplinary expiration. The stem does not describe a suspended or revoked license, and Board-specific conditions should not be converted into a universal NAPLEX requirement.

questions.citation: 247 CMR 4.02(3)-(5); Massachusetts Board of Registration in Pharmacy, Pharmacist Licensing: License Reactivation

questions.topic: Chlamydia EPT: paper prescription, unnamed partner and separate patient record
questions.stem: A patient diagnosed with chlamydia brings two separate, otherwise valid prescriptions from an authorized Massachusetts practitioner: one for the patient's own treatment and a signed paper prescription for an unexamined sex partner. The second prescription uses 'EPT' instead of the partner's name and address. The partner's identity is unavailable. The pharmacist has no clinical reason to withhold the appropriately prescribed Schedule VI therapy. Which dispensing approach is BEST supported by Massachusetts requirements?

choices.text: Request a replacement electronic prescription identifying the partner by name and address before dispensing the partner's treatment.
choices.why: The EPT framework expressly permits 'Expedited Partner Therapy,' 'E.P.T.' or 'EPT' in place of the partner's name and address. An otherwise lawful paper EPT prescription is also covered by the ePrescribing exception in 105 CMR 721.070(A)(7); a replacement is not necessary solely for these features.

choices.text: Fill both prescriptions under the diagnosed patient's profile and place the patient's name on both labels because that patient is collecting the drugs.
choices.why: The partner's treatment requires its own prescription and appropriate EPT profile and label. The collecting patient's identity should not be substituted as the treated recipient merely because the patient presents both prescriptions.

choices.text: Process the partner's separate prescription using an EPT patient profile and an EPT label rather than substituting the diagnosed patient's identity.
choices.why: Board/Drug Control Program Policy 2020-08 permits a separate EPT prescription for chlamydia with 'EPT' replacing the partner's name and address and directs creation of the corresponding EPT patient profile and prescription label. The absence of a direct examination is intrinsic to authorized EPT, not an automatic reason for refusal.

choices.text: Require confirmation that the practitioner examined the partner before dispensing, even though the prescription is expressly designated EPT.
choices.why: The Massachusetts EPT policy concerns treatment of the sex partner of a person diagnosed with chlamydia without examining or testing that partner. Requiring a prior examination in every such case would defeat this specifically authorized pathway. Clinical concerns must still be addressed when present.

questions.citation: MA Board/DCP Policy 2020-08, sections I-II; 105 CMR 721.020(D)(4) and 721.070(A)(7); 105 CMR 700.003 EPT provision

questions.topic: HIPAA access to one's own records: fees, electronic format and off-site storage
questions.stem: An adult submits a valid request directly to a HIPAA-covered Massachusetts pharmacy for an electronic PDF copy of the adult's own prescription and billing records. The records belong to the designated record set and are held electronically by the pharmacy's business associate. A PDF is readily producible. Identity has been verified, but the patient owes an unrelated unpaid prescription bill. No permitted ground for denying access or special confidentiality restriction applies. Considering the federal HIPAA access rule, which statements are correct? SELECT ALL THAT APPLY.

choices.text: The pharmacy may withhold the records until the patient pays the outstanding prescription bill, even if any lawful copying charge has been paid.
choices.why: HHS expressly states that unpaid charges for health care services are not a basis for denying an individual's access to their own PHI. Any permissible copying fee is a separate matter and does not turn the unrelated prescription debt into a lawful access condition.

choices.text: Any fee charged for the copy must be reasonable and cost-based; permitted copying labor may be included, but search and retrieval costs may not.
choices.why: 45 CFR 164.524(c)(4) limits an individual's copy fee to specified costs, including copying labor and applicable supplies or postage. HHS clarifies that searching for and retrieving the records are not chargeable components of this individual-access fee. This request is for the patient's own copy, not a third-party records request.

choices.text: The pharmacy must provide the electronic PDF requested rather than insist on paper solely for administrative convenience.
choices.why: Under 45 CFR 164.524(c)(2)(ii), electronically maintained PHI must be provided in the requested electronic form and format when readily producible. The stem establishes that PDF is readily producible, so convenience alone does not justify substituting paper.

choices.text: Because the business associate holds the records off-site, the pharmacy automatically has 60 days to respond without sending an extension notice.
choices.why: The ordinary outer limit is 30 calendar days from receipt of the request, including when records are held by a business associate. Only one extension of up to 30 additional days is available when needed, with written reasons and a completion date provided within the initial period. Off-site storage does not automatically grant 60 days.

questions.citation: 45 CFR 164.524(b)(2), (c)(2)(ii), (c)(4); HHS individual-access FAQs on unpaid bills, fees and business-associate records

questions.topic: Schedule II stock-shortage partial fill: elapsed hours across a weekend
questions.stem: A Massachusetts pharmacy receives an otherwise valid in-state electronic Schedule II prescription for 60 tablets. At 4:00 p.m. Friday, it dispenses its only 10 tablets and records a partial fill solely because of insufficient stock. The patient is not terminally ill or an LTCF resident. Neither the patient nor prescriber has requested a partial fill under the separate request-based pathway. The remaining stock arrives at 5:00 p.m. Monday; no clock change occurred over the weekend. What is the MOST appropriate action under the stock-shortage partial-fill provision?

choices.text: Dispense the remaining 50 tablets under the original prescription because fewer than 30 days have elapsed since it was issued.
choices.why: The separate 30-day request-based pathway is not the documented basis for this partial fill. Under 21 CFR 1306.13(a), the stock-shortage balance must be supplied within 72 hours of the first partial filling; the stem expressly excludes the other pathways.

choices.text: Start a new 72-hour completion period when the shipment arrives and dispense the balance within that new period.
choices.why: The shortage deadline runs from the first partial dispensing, not from replenishment or the date the pharmacist learns that stock is available. New inventory does not restart the clock.

choices.text: Dispense the balance because Saturday and Sunday are excluded when calculating the 72-hour completion period.
choices.why: The regulation specifies 72 hours, not 72 business hours. Friday at 4:00 p.m. to Monday at 5:00 p.m. is 73 elapsed hours when no clock change occurs, so the shortage-completion period has ended.

choices.text: Do not dispense the remaining balance under the original shortage partial fill; notify the prescriber, and obtain a new prescription before supplying any further quantity.
choices.why: 21 CFR 1306.13(a) requires prescriber notification when the balance is not or cannot be filled within 72 hours and states that no further quantity may be supplied beyond that period without a new prescription. The state request-based rule in 105 CMR 721.055 is a distinct route, not an automatic extension of this shortage fill.

questions.topic: Controlled-drug collection: patient returns versus pharmacy inventory and sealed liners
questions.stem: A Massachusetts retail pharmacy has modified its DEA registration to become an authorized collector and meets applicable state and environmental requirements. Its patient drug-collection receptacle is at the pharmacy's registered premises, not at an LTCF. The inner liner needs replacement. Separately, the pharmacy has expired Schedule II stock that has never been dispensed to a patient. Which procedures comply with the federal disposal rules? SELECT ALL THAT APPLY.

choices.text: Place the expired pharmacy stock into the patient collection receptacle after documenting a deduction from the pharmacy's inventory.
choices.why: A patient collection receptacle is not a disposal route for the registrant's own controlled-substance inventory. The pharmacy must use an authorized registrant-disposal method under 21 CFR 1317.05(a), such as transfer to a reverse distributor; an inventory entry does not convert the stock into an ultimate-user return.

choices.text: Have the inner liner installed and removed by, or under the supervision of, at least two collector employees, and have two employees seal it immediately upon removal.
choices.why: For this on-site retail receptacle, 21 CFR 1317.75(g) requires at least two collector employees for installation/removal or their supervision. Section 1317.60(c) additionally requires two employees to seal the liner immediately after removal. The separate LTCF staffing rules are not the scenario presented.

choices.text: Reopen the sealed liner with two pharmacist witnesses to count the controlled substances before sending it for destruction.
choices.why: Two witnesses do not create an exception to the prohibition. Under 21 CFR 1317.60(c), a sealed liner must not be opened, x-rayed, analyzed or otherwise penetrated. Section 1317.75(c) also prohibits counting, sorting or inventorying individual contents after deposit.

choices.text: Arrange a lawful transfer of the pharmacy's expired stock to a registered reverse distributor separately from the ultimate-user collection process.
choices.why: 21 CFR 1317.05(a)(2) authorizes disposal of practitioner inventory through delivery to a reverse distributor by the permitted pickup/carrier arrangements. Applicable controlled-substance transfer records and state requirements still apply; this is distinct from accepting patients' medications into a collection receptacle.
